title: Google's credit backstops become the hidden scaffolding of Anthropic's build-out
subtitle: New filings and reporting show Google is standing behind Anthropic's long-term lease obligations at TeraWulf's 401 MW Kentucky campus, extending a financing pattern that now underpins tens of billions in Anthropic infrastructure.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: TeraWulf disclosures and follow-up reporting this week clarify how Google is helping Anthropic finance its physical footprint: by standing behind Anthropic's lease obligations rather than putting cash on Anthropic's own balance sheet. The most recent example is the 401 MW Justified Data campus in Hawesville, Kentucky — a former aluminum smelter site where TeraWulf signed a 20-year, roughly $19 billion lease with Anthropic in July. Google's credit profile helps that lease clear investment-grade thresholds that neither TeraWulf nor Anthropic could reach alone.

The pattern is bigger than one site. Bloomberg Law has reported that Google's backstops underpin roughly $35 billion in compute capacity for Anthropic across five data centers — part of the $200 billion commercial relationship the two companies struck earlier this year. At TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in New York, Google took warrants for about 14 percent of TeraWulf's equity in exchange for $3.2 billion of lease support behind Fluidstack, whose capacity flows to Anthropic customers.

That is an unusual arrangement between two companies that also sell competing frontier models. For Anthropic, the structure lets it sign 10-plus-gigawatt infrastructure commitments without Google-scale cash reserves. For Google, it both earns commercial returns from TPU sales and compute leases and ensures Anthropic — a key Google Cloud customer and TPU consumer — can keep buying. The accounting fiction of 'competitor' blurs when financing works this way.

A takeaway for learners: in AI, the interesting money is no longer the model-training round. It is the twenty-year lease, the warrant package, and the credit backstop that lets a lab commit to gigawatts before it has the revenue to support them. When you read that a company 'signed a $19 billion deal,' the real question is who is on the hook if the revenue doesn't show up — because that is who actually owns the risk.
